title: Quantum I
subtitle: Probability, amplitudes and wave mechanics
prerequisites: Mathematical toolkit, Classical mechanics, Electricity & magnetism and Waves. Calculus, complex numbers, ODEs, Fourier transforms, inner products and eigenvectors are used; each lesson links local preparation. Numerical shooting and spherical/radial coordinates are bridged locally.
coverage: Three dimensions and orbital angular momentum

lessons.title: One photon has a frequency-dependent energy
lessons.idea: Making light brighter and changing its frequency are different ways to change the input.
body: Imagine shining monochromatic light on a clean material that can release electrons. Monochromatic means one frequency, or a very narrow range. In the simple one-photon photoelectric model, one absorbed photon supplies energy E_γ=hf. Here h is Planck’s constant and f is frequency.

Some energy is needed to remove the electron. Call that material-dependent work function W₀. The largest outgoing kinetic energy is K_max=hf−W₀ when the photon energy reaches the threshold. If hf<W₀, this one-photon model predicts no emitted electron; it does not predict an electron with negative kinetic energy.

A stopping voltage of magnitude V_s removes energy eV_s from the fastest emitted electrons, so eV_s=K_max. The symbol e is the positive elementary-charge magnitude; the electron charge is −e. An electronvolt, eV, is an energy unit: 1 eV=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J. It is not the same quantity as an electric potential measured in volts.

At fixed frequency, brighter light ordinarily supplies more photons per second, not more energy in each photon. In this low-intensity one-photon model that can increase the emitted count when emission is possible, but not K_max. Very intense multiphoton processes and detailed material effects are outside this simple model.
lessons.terms: E_γ, K_max, W₀: Photon energy, largest emitted kinetic energy and work function (J or eV, consistently). γ labels a photon; W₀ is energy, not power in watts. No emitted state is implied when hf<W₀. h, f: Planck constant and frequency (J·s, Hz). h=6.62607015×10⁻³⁴ J·s exactly by SI definition. In worked eV examples use rounded h≈4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s. e, V_s: Positive elementary charge and stopping-voltage magnitude (C, V). e=1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C exactly. The charge of an electron is −e. steps: Use f=8.00×10¹⁴ Hz, W₀=2.20 eV and the declared rounded h=4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s. One photon has energy 3.3088 eV.
The largest emitted kinetic energy is 3.3088−2.20=1.1088 eV. The stopping-voltage magnitude is therefore 1.1088 V, because one elementary charge crossing one volt changes energy by one electronvolt.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can a quoted work function be used for every material surface?
apply.answer: No. It depends on the material and its surface condition. A model calculation needs the stated W₀ and the regime where the one-photon energy balance is appropriate. It is not a universal electron-removal energy for all matter.

lessons.limits: One-photon photoelectric regime, stated clean-surface work function and narrow incident frequency. No multiphoton, detailed solid-state or practical safety claim.

lessons.title: A photon can transfer momentum as well as energy
lessons.idea: Changing a photon’s direction can leave less energy in that photon and more in an electron.
body: A photon in vacuum has momentum magnitude p_γ=E_γ/c=h/λ. When it scatters from an electron, conserve both total energy and vector momentum. The outgoing photon can have a longer wavelength and smaller energy while the electron recoils.

For a free electron initially at rest, the result is λ′−λ=(h/(m_ec))(1−cosθ). Theta is the angle between incoming and outgoing photon directions. A prime marks the outgoing wavelength. The factor h/(m_ec) is the electron’s Compton wavelength, about 2.426 pm; it is not the electron’s physical diameter.

This result uses relativistic energy and momentum, not the approximation K=p²/(2m) for every recoil. The relativistic relation used is E_total²=(pc)²+(m_ec²)², with E_total including rest energy. We use this supplied relation here; the separate Relativity path develops its derivation.

For example, at p=0 the relation gives rest energy E_total=m_ec². At p=m_ec it gives E_total=√2 m_ec², so kinetic energy is (√2−1)m_ec² rather than E_total itself. The photon’s lost energy equals the electron’s gained kinetic energy under the stated two-body assumptions.
lessons.terms: p_γ, p: Photon and electron momentum magnitudes (kg·m/s). p without γ refers to electron recoil in the relativistic relation. λ, λ′, θ: Incoming/outgoing wavelengths and scattering angle (m, m, degrees in examples). θ compares photon directions; 0° is forward and 180° backward. m_e, c, h: Electron rest mass, vacuum speed and Planck constant (kg, m/s, J·s). Use rounded m_e≈9.109×10⁻³¹ kg, c≈3.000×10⁸ m/s and Compton wavelength≈2.426 pm in simple examples. E_total, m_ec²: Electron total and rest energy (J or eV consistently). Electron rest energy is about 511 keV; keV means 1,000 eV. Kinetic energy is total minus rest energy. steps: Let the incident wavelength be 50.0 pm and photon scattering angle 90°. Since cos 90°=0, the wavelength increase is 2.426 pm and λ′=52.426 pm.
Using the declared rounded hc≈1240 eV·nm, the photon starts at 1240/0.0500=24,800 eV. It leaves with about 1240/0.052426≈23,652 eV.

check.prompt: In the same free-electron model, θ=60°. What is the wavelength increase using 2.426 pm for the Compton scale?
explanations: That is the backward-scattering shift, not the 60° shift.
At 60°, 1−cosθ=1/2 rather than 1.
Correct. Multiply 2.426 pm by 1−0.5 to get 1.213 pm.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would the same simple formula automatically apply to a strongly bound moving electron?
apply.answer: No. The derivation assumes an initially resting free electron. Binding, initial momentum and other interactions can change the observed energy distribution. State those assumptions before using the free-electron relation.

lessons.limits: Free electron initially at rest and a single photon scattering event in vacuum. Relativistic energy-momentum conservation is a supplied law here; this is not a derivation of relativity or a classical electron-size measurement.

lessons.title: Use momentum to set a matter-wave scale
lessons.idea: A de Broglie wavelength belongs to a quantum state’s momentum scale, not to a little object’s diameter.
body: Quantum experiments with electrons and other matter show interference effects whose scale is described by λ=h/p. For a slow particle with a narrow momentum spread, p≈mv and kinetic energy K≈p²/(2m). “Slow” here means speed much smaller than the vacuum light speed c.

These relations give p≈√(2mK) and λ≈h/√(2mK). Use energy in joules with h in J·s and mass in kilograms. If energy is supplied in electronvolts, convert it first. The approximation must be rechecked for highly energetic electrons.

A state sharply specified in momentum is spread out in position; it is not a tiny water wave attached to a bead. A localized state needs a range of momentum components, which we will describe with a wavefunction and packet. The wavelength tells a phase scale of those components, not an observed path.

The relation uses momentum magnitude; it does not name a physical particle width. m, K: Particle mass and nonrelativistic kinetic energy (kg, J). K=p²/(2m) is an approximation when speed is much less than c. h, e: Planck constant and elementary-charge magnitude (J·s, C). Use rounded h=6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s and 1 eV≈1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J for this example. √, ≈: Nonnegative square root and approximately equal (no unit). The approximation is physical as well as numerical: it excludes relativistic speeds. check.prompt: Under the same nonrelativistic assumptions, mass stays fixed and kinetic energy becomes nine times as large. What happens to λ?
options: It becomes one third as large
It becomes one ninth as large
It becomes three times as large
explanations: Correct. Momentum scales with √K, so it triples and λ=h/p becomes one third.
The square root makes the energy-to-momentum scaling different from a direct ratio.
Higher momentum gives shorter, not longer, wavelength.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why is a short wavelength not proof that all quantum effects disappear?
apply.answer: It says only that this phase scale is short for the stated momentum. Whether interference or other quantum effects matter also depends on preparation, coherence, environment and the experimental length/time scales. Compare those scales instead of using wavelength alone as a universal on/off switch.

lessons.limits: Nonrelativistic momentum-energy approximation, positive kinetic energy and stated particle mass. A single characteristic wavelength assumes an adequately narrow momentum distribution.

lessons.title: Separate one detection from many-run statistics
lessons.idea: A pattern built from repeated detections does not tell you a unique path for each event.
body: Imagine an ideal repeated experiment that prepares the same state, then records one localized detector outcome each run. A single run gives one result, while many runs reveal a distribution. An interference pattern concerns that distribution, not each event splitting into several recorded detections.

If an outcome region has probability p and there are N independent identical preparations, the expected count is Np. Expected means the average over many repeated batches, not an exact count guaranteed in one batch. For independent yes/no outcomes, the count standard deviation is √[Np(1−p)]. A standard deviation describes a statistical spread, not a fixed maximum error.

When alternatives remain coherent, their amplitudes can interfere. A setup that records distinguishable path information changes which alternatives can interfere. That does not by itself establish a classical trajectory between preparation and detection. We will calculate amplitudes next rather than attach an untested picture of a path.
lessons.equation: Expected count= Np;  count standard deviation=√[Np(1−p)]
lessons.terms: N, p: Number of independent runs and region probability (count, no unit). N is a positive integer and 0≤p≤1. Each run uses the same preparation and measurement. Np: Expected detection count (count). It can be noninteger as an average, even though an actual batch count is an integer. √[Np(1−p)]: Count standard deviation (count). This binomial formula assumes independent trials with the same probability; it is not a certainty interval. example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Suppose a specified detector region has probability p=0.25 and we perform N=400 independent runs.
Expected count is 400×0.25=100. The count standard deviation is √(400×0.25×0.75)=√75≈8.66.

An observed count of 96 is not a contradiction of p=0.25 merely because it is not exactly 100. Deciding whether data challenge a model requires a stated statistical test and its assumptions, not exact equality with the mean.

check.prompt: For p=0.25 and N=100 independent runs, is exactly 25 detections guaranteed?
options: Yes, because probability fixes every batch
No; probability cannot predict any averages
explanations: Probability describes a distribution of possible batch counts.
Correct. A finite batch can fluctuate; Np=25 is its mean, not a forced outcome.
The model does predict means and fluctuation statistics under its assumptions.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If a plotted pattern changes after adding path detection, can one keep the old state-and-measurement model unchanged?
apply.answer: No. Recording path information changes the physical setup and the state/measurement description. Recompute the relevant probabilities for the new setup. The before-and-after patterns do not license guessing an unseen classical path without an additional justified model.

lessons.limits: Independent identically prepared runs and idealized detection probabilities. Real inefficiency, drift, correlated trials and background counts require separate modelling.

practice.reasoning: Explain why a mean of 45 does not require observing exactly 45 in one batch. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Use a complex number before asking for a probability
lessons.idea: A quantum amplitude stores both a size and a relative phase.
body: Consider an ideal measurement with two distinct outcomes, labelled 0 and 1. Choose orthonormal basis states u₀ and u₁ for those outcomes. Orthonormal means each has length one in the inner-product sense, and their overlap is zero.

Write the state as ψ=c₀u₀+c₁u₁, or as the coefficient column (c₀,c₁) in this chosen basis. The coefficients are complex amplitudes. A complex number a+ib has real part a and imaginary part b, with i²=−1. It is not itself a probability.

The squared magnitude is |a+ib|²=(a−ib)(a+ib)=a²+b². The star in c* means complex conjugate: change the sign of the imaginary part. For a normalized two-outcome state, |c₀|²+|c₁|²=1. The next step connects those squared sizes to measurement probabilities.
lessons.terms: ψ, u₀, u₁: State and chosen orthonormal basis states (no physical unit in this finite-dimensional representation). These are abstract state vectors, not ordinary spatial arrows. c₀, c₁, c: Complex coefficients (no unit). Subscripts label basis components; coefficients can have negative or imaginary parts. *, |c|², i: Conjugation, squared magnitude and imaginary unit (no unit). Conjugation changes i to−i; i²=−1. The expression c* · c means c* multiplied by c. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), C coulomb (charge), V volt (joules per coulomb), rad radian (angle). nm=10⁻⁹ m; pm=10⁻¹² m. steps: Take c₀=3/5 and c₁=4i/5. The second coefficient is imaginary, but that does not imply an imaginary probability.
Squared sizes are |c₀|²=9/25=0.36 and |c₁|²=16/25=0.64.
Their sum is 1, so this coefficient column is normalized. Replacing c₁ by−4i/5 leaves its squared size unchanged but changes the relative phase.

explanations: Correct. Square the real and imaginary parts:1/4+1/4=1/2.
That is the amplitude, not its squared magnitude.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Can the same coefficient column be interpreted without naming the measurement basis?
apply.answer: Not completely. The entries say how much of each chosen basis state appears. A different basis generally gives different coefficients for the same physical state. Keep the basis labels and the measurement model attached to the numbers.

glossary.definition: A complex coefficient used to calculate outcome probabilities and interference.
A chosen set of independent state directions used to describe other states.

lessons.title: Square amplitudes in the chosen outcome basis
lessons.idea: The Born rule turns normalized amplitudes into probabilities for a specified measurement.
body: For an ideal measurement whose orthonormal outcome states are u_j, the probability of outcome j is P(j)=|c_j|² when ψ=Σ_j c_j u_j is normalized. The symbol Σ means add over all listed outcomes. This rule is part of the quantum model, not a deduction from ordinary classical counting alone.

Each probability is nonnegative and their sum is 1. That does not mean the individual result is predetermined by these probabilities in the model. It means the model gives a distribution for identically prepared measurements.

If the numerical vector is not yet normalized, divide each coefficient by its norm N=√(Σ_j|c_j|²), provided N is nonzero. Here N names a norm, not the number of trials used in the preceding experiment. A zero vector cannot describe a normalized state.
lessons.terms: P(j), c_j, j: Outcome probability, basis coefficient and outcome index (no unit). The chosen measurement basis must be orthonormal and complete for the listed state space. Σ_j, N: Sum over outcomes and vector norm (no unit). N here is the positive length of the coefficient vector, not a trial count. √: Nonnegative square root (no unit). The zero vector has N=0 and cannot be normalized. check.prompt: A normalized state has coefficients (√3/2,−i/2). What is P(1)?
explanations: Probability uses squared magnitude, so it cannot be negative here.
The amplitude magnitude is 1/2; probability squares it.
Correct. |−i/2|²=1/4.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If both entries of an unnormalized vector are multiplied by 10, does normalization change the predicted probabilities?
apply.answer: No. The norm also grows by 10 in magnitude, so the normalized vector differs at most by a common phase if the multiplier is complex. Relative coefficients determine the normalized state; arbitrary overall size does not change its probabilities.

lessons.title: A density is not the probability at one point
lessons.idea: For position, add probability density over a region to get a probability.
body: A position wavefunction ψ(x) assigns a complex amplitude to each position coordinate x. In one dimension, the Born density is ρ(x)=|ψ(x)|². The probability of finding position between a and b is P[a,b]=∫ₐᵇρ(x)dx.

Because probability has no unit and dx has units of length, ρ has units of inverse length and ψ has units of inverse square root of length. With metres as the coordinate unit, those are m⁻¹ and m⁻¹ᐟ². A density value can exceed 1 without any probability exceeding 1.

For a continuous nonsingular density, a single exact point has zero interval length and hence zero probability, even if the density there is large. Actual detectors report finite resolution regions, not an exact mathematical coordinate with infinitely many digits. Density describes how probability is packed per unit length.

These units apply to a normalized one-dimensional position representation. x, a, b, dx: Position, interval endpoints and small integration length (m). a≤b; dx is part of the integral, not an extra particle property. P[a,b], ∫: Interval probability and continuous sum (no unit for probability). Integrate density, not raw complex amplitude, for a position interval probability. example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For a simple probability example, let density be 5 m⁻¹ over a 0.20 m interval and zero elsewhere. Its integral is(5 m⁻¹)(0.20 m)=1.
A0.030 m subinterval inside that region has probability 0.15. The density is numerically 5, but the integrated probability is still between 0 and 1.

This compact probability example says nothing yet about finite kinetic energy or Hamiltonian boundary conditions. A sharp-edged wavefunction can be a mathematical probability state without satisfying every later differential-operator requirement.

check.prompt: Uniform density is 4 m⁻¹ over a valid normalized region. What is the probability in a 0.05 m subinterval entirely inside it?
explanations: Correct. Multiply 4 m⁻¹ by 0.05 m to obtain 0.20.
That is a density value, not an integrated probability.
The interval length alone is not the probability unless the numerical density is 1 in matching units.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would changing coordinate units from metres to centimetres leave the numerical density unchanged?
apply.answer: No. Probability stays the same, but probability per centimetre is one hundredth of probability per metre for the same distribution. The density’s number changes with its length unit so that integrating over the corresponding interval gives the same probability.

lessons.title: Change all phases together or change one relative phase
lessons.idea: A common phase is unobservable, while relative phase can change another measurement’s probabilities.
body: Multiply every amplitude by the same number e^(iα), whose magnitude is 1. This is a global phase change. All probabilities and expectation values are unchanged because the common phase and its conjugate cancel in those quantities. An overlap amplitude with a fixed basis vector can acquire that common phase, but its squared magnitude does not change.

By contrast, changing one coefficient’s phase relative to another can change interference. For two basis states u₀ and u₁, compare ψ_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 with ψ_-=(u₀−u₁)/√2. Measuring in the original basis gives probability 1/2 for each outcome in either state.

Now choose the alternate orthonormal outcome u_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 and its partner u_-=(u₀−u₁)/√2. The amplitude for the plus outcome is the inner product ⟨u_+,ψ⟩, which conjugates the first vector’s coefficients. Its probability is |⟨u_+,ψ⟩|². In this basis the two states are perfectly distinguishable.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: If two states have the same probabilities in one basis, must they be the same physical state?
apply.answer: No. Their relative phases may differ, and another measurement can distinguish them. One basis’s outcome frequencies do not generally determine an entire quantum state. A global phase is the exception: it does not change any observable probability.

lessons.title: Choose the scale so total probability is one
lessons.idea: Normalization fixes the overall size of a nonzero wavefunction without changing its shape.
body: Take a function on 0≤x≤L of the form ψ(x)=A sin(πx/L). Outside this interval it is zero. The unknown A sets amplitude size; x/L has no unit, so the sine argument is a valid angle. This is a mathematical state example; a later lesson derives when it is an energy eigenstate of a specific well.

Total probability must satisfy 1=|A|²∫₀ᴸsin²(πx/L)dx. The integral is L/2: the identity sin²u=(1−cos 2u)/2 turns it into a constant part plus an oscillating part that integrates to zero over this interval.

Therefore |A|=√(2/L). We may choose A positive and real because its common phase would not change probabilities. A has units m⁻¹ᐟ² if L is in metres. A zero function cannot be normalized because its norm stays zero under every finite scaling.

lessons.title: Integrate the part of the density you care about
lessons.idea: Equal-length position intervals need not have equal probabilities.
body: Use the normalized sine state ψ(x)=√(2/L)sin(πx/L) on 0≤x≤L. Its density isρ(x)=(2/L)sin²(πx/L), largest near the centre and zero at the endpoints.

The probability from a to b inside the interval is P[a,b]=(b−a)/L−[sin(2πb/L)−sin(2πa/L)]/(2π). This comes from integrating the sine-squared identity used for normalization. Each term has no unit; a,b and L must be in matching length units.

The first term alone would be the answer for a uniform density. The sine correction records that this state is not uniform. Integrating over a region is a position measurement rule; it is not adding amplitudes from distinct positions and squaring the result.

lessons.title: A Gaussian gives a smooth localized position distribution
lessons.idea: Its width must be defined from probability, not guessed from the amplitude exponent.
body: Choose centre x₀ and positive position standard deviation σ. Write ψ(x)=(2πσ²)^(−1/4) exp[−(x−x₀)²/(4σ²)], a real positive amplitude. The exponent is dimensionless because both its numerator and denominator have units of length squared.

Squaring givesρ(x)=1/(√(2π)σ) exp[−(x−x₀)²/(2σ²)]. This is the normalized Gaussian probability density with mean x₀ and standard deviation σ. The amplitude and density have different exponents; forgetting the square creates a width error.

To check normalization, set u=(x−x₀)/σ. Then dx=σdu, and use the standard Gaussian integral∫ from−∞ to∞ exp(−u²/2)du=√(2π). This integral identity is supplied here; it is not an elementary antiderivative. It makes the total density integral exactly 1.

lessons.title: Overlap is a weighted sum of amplitudes
lessons.idea: Two states can be orthogonal even when both are nonzero in the same region.
body: For functions on the same position domain, define⟨u,v⟩=∫u*(x)v(x)dx. Conjugate the first function before multiplying. The integral is a complex overlap amplitude, not the probability of a position interval.

On 0≤x≤L, let u₁=√(2/L)sin(πx/L) and u₂=√(2/L)sin(2πx/L). Each has norm 1. Their overlap is zero: positive and negative products cancel across the interval. Orthogonal does not mean their spatial supports are disjoint.

For ψ=(u₁+i u₂)/√2, projection gives⟨u₁,ψ⟩=1/√2 and⟨u₂,ψ⟩=i/√2. In an ideal measurement with these outcome states, the probabilities are each 1/2. Reversing the inner-product arguments conjugates the result, so keep the order clear.

lessons.title: Project a state onto a complete basis
lessons.idea: A basis lets us reconstruct a state from coefficients, provided we keep the full required set.
body: For a complete orthonormal basis u_j in the chosen state space, the coefficient is c_j=⟨u_j,ψ⟩ and the state is ψ=Σ_jc_ju_j. “Complete” means every state in this model can be built from the basis; it does not mean a finite list describes every physical system.

Orthonormality removes cross terms from the total norm, so⟨ψ,ψ⟩=Σ_j|c_j|². A normalized state has a sum of 1. Individual components are mathematical basis contributions, not a claim that an unmeasured system secretly occupies one particular basis state.

If an approximation keeps only some basis terms, the retained squared norm can be less than 1. That missing weight matters. Renormalizing the retained terms creates a new normalized approximation, or a conditional state after a specified selection; it does not leave the original state unchanged.

body: Use two real normalized orthogonal position functions u₁ and u₂ and the state ψ=(u₁+e^(iφ)u₂)/√2. The relative phase φ can affect position density even though both basis weights remain 1/2.

Multiplying ψ by its conjugate givesρ=½u₁²+½u₂²+u₁u₂cosφ. The last part is the interference cross term. It can be positive or negative, but the total density remains nonnegative because it is |ψ|². Its integral over all space is 1 because the cross integral vanishes for orthogonal functions.

For a position interval, integrate the whole density, including the cross term. Adding separate basis probabilities alone would discard coherence and describe a different preparation. A density value at one point is still not the probability of that exact point.

lessons.title: Two preparations can share one outcome distribution
lessons.idea: A coherent superposition and a random mixture are different preparation procedures.
body: Preparation A makes the same coherent state ψ_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 on every run. Preparation B uses a classical random choice: half the runs prepare u₀ and half prepare u₁. The choice is not kept as usable information in the measured ensemble.

Both preparations give probabilities 1/2 and 1/2 in the original(u₀,u₁) measurement. But their alternate-basis statistics differ. The plus outcome u_+=(u₀+u₁)/√2 occurs with probability 1 for preparation A.

For the mixture, average the probabilities of its different prepared states, not their amplitudes. Each component u₀ oru₁ gives plus probability 1/2, so P_mix(+)=½×½+½×½=1/2. A coherent sum contains a relative-phase cross term; this mixture has no such stable cross term.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: For the coherent plus state, measuring in the plus/minus basis gives P(+)=1 and P(−)=0.
For a 50/50 mixture of u₀ and u₁, each component has P(+)=1/2. The mixture therefore gives P(+)=1/2 and P(−)=1/2.

check.prompt: If two preparations give the same original-basis probabilities, can you conclude one is a coherent superposition?
options: No; another measurement may be needed
Yes, if the probabilities sum to 1
explanations: A mixture can give the same original-basis distribution.
Correct. Coherence is revealed by suitable phase-sensitive measurements, not one distribution alone.
Normalization is necessary for both coherent states and mixtures.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why is forgetting a classical preparation label not the same operation as adding two state amplitudes?
apply.answer: Forgetting the label makes us average the probabilities from alternatives that were randomly chosen on separate runs. Coherent addition refers to a single prepared state with a definite relative-phase relation between components. The operational predictions can differ, as the alternate-basis example shows.

lessons.limits: Finite idealized state preparations and projective outcome bases. General mixed-state density operators, environment entanglement and decoherence dynamics are developed later; no claim that all mixtures arise only from conscious ignorance.

lessons.title: Condition on an ideal measurement result
lessons.idea: After an ideal projective outcome, keep the matching state component and normalize it.
body: For this lesson, assume an ideal nondegenerate projective measurement with orthonormal outcome states u_j. Nondegenerate means one state direction per outcome. The probability is P(j)=|⟨u_j,ψ⟩|². If outcome j is recorded with nonzero probability, the conditional state becomes u_j up to an irrelevant common phase.

The operation can be written P_jψ=u_j⟨u_j,ψ⟩: keep just the component along u_j. The normalized conditional state is ψ_after=P_jψ/√P(j). Here P_j is a projection operator while P(j) is a number; the similar letter must not hide that difference.

This is the ideal update rule being used, not a derivation of every measurement process. If the same measurement is immediately repeated with no intervening evolution or disturbance, it gives the same outcome with probability 1. A different measurement basis can again have several possible outcomes.
lessons.terms: ψ, ψ_after, u_j: Initial state, conditional state and outcome basis state (no unit in this abstract representation). The outcome is conditioned on an actual recorded result; no prediction of a guaranteed initial result is implied. P(j), P_j: Outcome probability and projection operator (number and state-space operation). P_j keeps one component; P(j) is its squared norm. They are different mathematical objects. ⟨u_j,ψ⟩, √P(j): Outcome amplitude and normalization factor (no unit). The conditional formula requires P(j)>0; a zero-probability event cannot be conditioned this way. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), C coulomb (charge), V volt (joules per coulomb), rad radian (angle). nm=10⁻⁹ m; pm=10⁻¹² m. A dot multiplies units; a slash means per. Bare arithmetic uses numerical values in the stated units. Symbols for quantities are defined separately from unit labels.

equationGuide.meaning: First compute the outcome probability. Conditional on recording a possible outcome, discard the other basis components and rescale the retained component to norm one.

steps: Let ψ=(3/5)u₀+(4/5)u₁. Measuring in this basis gives outcome 1 with probability 16/25=0.64.
If outcome 1 occurs, P₁ψ=(4/5)u₁ and dividing by √0.64=4/5 gives ψ_after=u₁.

An immediate same-basis repeat then yields 1 with certainty in the ideal model. A plus/minus-basis measurement instead gives 1/2 for each outcome because u₁ has equal-magnitude projections in that basis.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Would the same simple one-direction update apply unchanged to a degenerate or non-projective measurement?
apply.answer: No. Degeneracy can leave a whole outcome subspace rather than one unique state direction, and more general measurements use other state-update operations. Keep this lesson’s ideal nondegenerate-projective assumptions attached to its certainty claim.

lessons.title: An equation changes the whole amplitude
lessons.idea: The wavefunction is a complex probability amplitude, not a little object’s path. The Schrödinger equation tells how that amplitude changes with time.
body: The wavefunction is a complex probability amplitude, not a little object’s path. The Schrödinger equation tells how that amplitude changes with time.

In one dimension, ψ(x,t) depends on position and time. A partial derivative changes one input while holding the other fixed. The second position derivative measures curvature, not probability. Multiply that curvature by −ℏ²/(2m), then add Vψ. This gives the energy operator’s action; multiplying the time derivative by iℏ gives the same result.

V is potential energy in joules, not voltage. The equation is a model for a nonrelativistic particle with constant positive mass and a specified scalar potential. It does not by itself say which initial state was prepared; that initial amplitude and the boundaries must also be supplied.
lessons.terms: ψ, x, t: wavefunction, position and time (m⁻¹ᐟ²; m; s). The squared magnitude integrates to one over the allowed position domain. m, V: particle mass and potential energy (kg; J). m as a quantity is mass, not the metre unit. ℏ, i, ∂: reduced Planck constant, imaginary unit and partial derivative (J·s; dimensionless; operator). Every term has units J·m⁻¹ᐟ². Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: At one point suppose the kinetic term vanishes and V=3.0×10⁻²¹ J. The equation there gives ∂ψ/∂t=−i(V/ℏ)ψ.
Using the stated rounded ℏ, V/ℏ≈2.84476×10¹³ s⁻¹. The local amplitude derivative is therefore −i times that rate times ψ.
This is a pointwise derivative statement, not a globally constant normalized state on the whole line.

apply.answer: No. First specify and evolve the normalized initial state, then integrate |ψ|² over that interval.

lessons.title: Apply the energy operator before naming an energy
lessons.idea: An operator is a rule that takes a function and produces another function. The Hamiltonian Ĥ is the energy operator in this model.
body: An operator is a rule that takes a function and produces another function. The Hamiltonian Ĥ is the energy operator in this model.
Ĥψ means differentiate ψ twice, multiply by −ℏ²/(2m), and add Vψ. It is not usually one constant times ψ. Only an energy eigenfunction obeys Ĥφ=Eφ with the same constant E everywhere on its domain.

For a concrete check choose the smooth shape φ(x)=C exp[−x²/(2L²)] on the whole line. C is a constant with amplitude units; choose it to normalize the shape if using probabilities. Its second derivative is (x²/L⁴−1/L²)φ. With V=0, dividing the result by φ shows a position-dependent factor, so this shape is not a free-particle energy eigenfunction.
lessons.equation: Ĥψ = −[ℏ²/(2m)]ψ″ + Vψ; Ĥφ = E₀[1−(x/L)²]φ for this free Gaussian; E₀=ℏ²/(2mL²)
lessons.terms: Ĥ, E₀: energy operator and positive energy scale (J as operator unit; J). The hat distinguishes a rule from an ordinary number. φ, C, L: trial amplitude, constant and width scale (m⁻¹ᐟ²; m⁻¹ᐟ²; m). L>0; prime means a position derivative. L here is not its probability standard deviation. m, x, V: mass, position and potential energy (kg; m; J). V=0 in the worked example. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Use L=1.0 nm and m=2.0×10⁻³⁰ kg. The rounded ℏ gives E₀≈2.78030×10⁻²¹ J.
At x=0, Ĥφ/φ=E₀. At x=L, that ratio is zero. At x=2L it is −3E₀≈−8.34091×10⁻²¹ J.
A negative pointwise ratio does not mean a measured free kinetic energy is negative. An expectation integrates ψ*Ĥψ over the full domain; a ratio at one point is not an outcome.

lessons.title: One energy adds one rotating phase
lessons.idea: When the potential does not change with time, try a wavefunction made of a spatial shape times a time factor.
body: When the potential does not change with time, try a wavefunction made of a spatial shape times a time factor.

Write ψ=φ(x)T(t), insert it into the time equation, and divide where the factors are nonzero. The time-only expression iℏT′/T equals the position-only expression Ĥφ/φ. Their common constant is E. Thus Ĥφ=Eφ and T′=−iET/ℏ.

Taking T(0)=1 gives T=exp(−iEt/ℏ). For a real energy, this factor has magnitude one. Therefore |ψ|²=|φ|²: the position density of a single energy state is stationary even though the amplitude’s phase changes. Boundary conditions select which E and φ are allowed.
lessons.terms: φ, ψ: spatial eigenfunction and evolving wavefunction (m⁻¹ᐟ²). Normalize a bound state on its physical domain. E, Ĥ: energy eigenvalue and Hamiltonian (J). The Hamiltonian and its domain are time independent. T, t: time factor and time (dimensionless; s). Et/ℏ is a dimensionless phase; T′ means a time derivative. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: Take an allowed eigenstate with E=2E₀, where E₀ is a positive reference energy. At t=πℏ/(4E₀), Et/ℏ=π/2.
Then T=exp(−iπ/2)=−i. The amplitude is multiplied by −i, while its squared magnitude is unchanged.
At twice that time the multiplier is −1, again with no change to the position density.

check.prompt: Does a stationary density mean the wavefunction is a constant real function?
options: No; a nontrivial shape can acquire a changing complex phase.
Yes; its energy must be zero.
explanations: Correct: density discards an overall phase, not all spatial structure.
The spatial and time derivatives need not vanish.
Any real allowed energy has a phase factor of magnitude one.

apply.answer: This fixed-energy separation need not work. The Hamiltonian’s changing action can mix the earlier energy components.

lessons.limits: Separation covers energy eigenstates of a time-independent self-adjoint Hamiltonian, not every initial state. Division is a derivation device; the final equations extend through zeros of φ.

lessons.title: Different energies rotate at different rates
lessons.idea: A superposition of different energies is not generally stationary. Each energy component gets its own time phase.
body: A superposition of different energies is not generally stationary. Each energy component gets its own time phase.

Let |1⟩ and |2⟩ be orthonormal energy states, with energies E₁ and E₂. The notation |j⟩ names a state, not a physical box. Prepare (|1⟩+|2⟩)/√2. After time t, the two coefficients are exp(−iE₁t/ℏ)/√2 and exp(−iE₂t/ℏ)/√2.

Now measure the projection onto |+⟩=(|1⟩+|2⟩)/√2. Add the two phase amplitudes and square their magnitude. The probability depends on the energy difference ΔE, not on a shared shift of both energies. This is a specified two-state measurement, not necessarily a position measurement.
lessons.terms: E₁, E₂, ΔE: two energies and their difference (J). Assume ΔE>0 in the time examples. |1⟩, |2⟩, |+⟩: normalized state vectors (dimensionless abstract vectors). Orthonormal means each has norm one and their overlap is zero. P₊, t: plus-outcome probability and time (dimensionless; s). The expectation of the plus projector equals this probability. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

steps: At t=0, the plus probability is 1.
At t=πℏ/(2ΔE), the relative phase is π/2 and P₊=1/2.
At t=πℏ/ΔE, P₊=0. Measuring energy instead still gives E₁ or E₂ with probabilities 1/2 each.

Correct: the added common phase cancels in probabilities.
P₊ is a probability between zero and one.

apply.text: Would a 50–50 incoherent mixture show this same oscillating P₊?

lessons.title: Keep account of probability crossing a boundary
lessons.idea: Probability inside an interval changes when probability flows through its ends. Current is the rate of that flow, not a guessed particle path.
body: Probability inside an interval changes when probability flows through its ends. Current is the rate of that flow, not a guessed particle path.

Set ρ=ψ*ψ. Differentiate this product in time. Use the Schrödinger equation for ψ and its complex conjugate for ψ*. For real V, the two potential terms cancel. The kinetic terms form a position derivative: ∂tρ=(iℏ/(2m))∂x(ψ*∂xψ−ψ∂xψ*). This equals −∂xj with the j below.

Integrating from a to b gives dP[a,b]/dt=j(a)−j(b). More entering at the left than leaving at the right increases the interval probability. Total norm is conserved when the endpoint currents agree, including vanishing currents at both infinities for suitable localized states.

Positive j means flow toward increasing x. Im, ∂x, ∂t: imaginary part and partial derivatives (operators). Im selects the imaginary component; a,b are interval endpoints in m. m, ℏ: mass and reduced Planck constant (kg; J·s). This formula assumes no vector potential. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

steps: If j(a)=0.30 s⁻¹ and j(b)=0.10 s⁻¹ at an instant, the interval probability increases at 0.20 s⁻¹.
For a local phase gradient ψ=C exp(ikx), the formula gives j=(ℏk/m)|C|². Let k=2.0×10⁹ m⁻¹, m=2.0×10⁻³⁰ kg and local density |C|²=1.0×10⁸ m⁻¹. Then j≈1.05457×10¹³ s⁻¹.

lessons.title: Position multiplies; momentum differentiates
lessons.idea: In the position description, the position operator multiplies the amplitude by x. The momentum operator differentiates it and multiplies by −iℏ.
body: In the position description, the position operator multiplies the amplitude by x. The momentum operator differentiates it and multiplies by −iℏ.

For a plane factor exp(ikx), one derivative brings down ik. Multiplying by −iℏ leaves ℏk times the same factor. This is the momentum-eigenvalue relation. On the entire line this plane wave is a generalized state, not a normalized square-integrable wavefunction.

For a localized Gaussian C exp[−x²/(2L²)], momentum instead produces iℏx/L² times that Gaussian. Because the factor depends on x, the Gaussian is not a momentum eigenfunction. Position multiplication and momentum differentiation are different actions, even though both start with the same function.

Hats mark rules acting on functions. x, k, L: position, wave number and Gaussian scale (m; m⁻¹; m). k may be positive or negative; L>0. ψ, ψ′: amplitude and position derivative (m⁻¹ᐟ²; m⁻³ᐟ²). The output p̂ψ has amplitude times momentum units. lessons.title: A differential rule also needs allowed functions
lessons.idea: A matrix and a differential expression need different amounts of information. A finite Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose; on the full finite vector space it defines a self-adjoint observable.
body: A matrix and a differential expression need different amounts of information. A finite Hermitian matrix equals its conjugate transpose; on the full finite vector space it defines a self-adjoint observable.

The domain is the set of allowed input functions, including boundary conditions. Symmetric means that moving the operator from one side of an inner product to the other gives the same result for every allowed pair. The adjoint is the operator defined by that inner-product relation on its full possible domain. Self-adjoint means both its action and its full domain agree with the original operator; a smaller domain can fail this test.

For a derivative, specify which functions and boundary conditions are allowed. Integrating momentum by parts gives a boundary term: ⟨f,p̂g⟩−⟨p̂f,g⟩=−iℏ[f*g]ₐᵇ. The bracket means the value at b minus the value at a. If it does not vanish for allowed pairs, this domain is not even symmetric.

On an interval of length L, periodic functions with square-integrable first derivative and f(L)=f(0) give one self-adjoint momentum choice. Forcing both endpoints to zero makes the boundary term vanish too, but the first-derivative operator on that smaller domain is not self-adjoint. A vanished boundary term alone is not the complete domain test.

Inner product integrates f*g over the declared interval. a, b, L, p̂: endpoints, interval length and momentum rule (m; kg·m/s for p̂). Both operator action and allowed domain are part of the observable. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

steps: Take A=E₀[[2,i],[−i,5]], with E₀>0 an energy unit. Conjugating and transposing returns the same matrix, so it is Hermitian.

If trial endpoint products instead differ by 2/L, the boundary term is −2iℏ/L, not zero. Such unrestricted trial functions cannot all belong to a symmetric momentum domain.

lessons.title: An average is not always an allowed outcome
lessons.idea: An expectation is the average predicted across many identically prepared measurements. A single result still comes from the observable’s allowed outcomes.
body: An expectation is the average predicted across many identically prepared measurements. A single result still comes from the observable’s allowed outcomes.

For outcome values aⱼ with probabilities Pⱼ, add Pⱼaⱼ to obtain the mean. Repeat with aⱼ² to obtain the second moment. Subtract the square of the mean to obtain variance; its nonnegative square root is the standard deviation.

For an admissible normalized wavefunction the same calculation is written ⟨A⟩=∫ψ*Âψ dx. The second moment uses Â² on a compatible domain. A finite variance requires these quantities to exist; a formal expression alone is not enough.

lessons.title: Changing the order can change the result
lessons.idea: A commutator compares two orders: [Â,B̂] means ÂB̂−B̂Â. Read each product from right to left: the rightmost rule acts first.
body: A commutator compares two orders: [Â,B̂] means ÂB̂−B̂Â. Read each product from right to left: the rightmost rule acts first.

Apply this to a smooth test function f for which both orders are allowed. x̂p̂f=−iℏxf′. The product rule gives p̂x̂f=−iℏ(f+xf′). Subtracting leaves iℏf. Thus [x̂,p̂]=iℏI on this common domain, with I the rule that leaves a function unchanged.

Finite matrices can also fail to commute. Unlike the canonical position/momentum relation, their commutator need not be a constant times the identity. Always apply the actual matrices in the chosen order.

For instance a smooth rapidly decaying function on the line fits the calculation. x̂, p̂, ℏ: position, momentum and action constant (m; kg·m/s; J·s). The commutator has position times momentum units, equal to action units. Therefore [A,B]u=(0,2). Reversing the commutator gives (0,−2).
For the continuum relation, take normalized f and form its expectation: ⟨[x̂,p̂]⟩=iℏ∫|f|²dx=iℏ, provided the common-domain conditions hold.

lessons.title: A mean can follow a force equation
lessons.idea: The average position and momentum can obey familiar-looking motion rules, but they describe averages of repeated preparations, not a revealed path of each particle.
body: The average position and momentum can obey familiar-looking motion rules, but they describe averages of repeated preparations, not a revealed path of each particle.

Differentiating an expectation and using Schrödinger evolution gives d⟨A⟩/dt=(i/ℏ)⟨[Ĥ,Â]⟩ when Â has no explicit time dependence and domains allow the calculation. For Ĥ=p̂²/(2m)+V(x), the commutators give d⟨x⟩/dt=⟨p⟩/m and d⟨p⟩/dt=−⟨V′(x)⟩.

The average force need not equal the force at the average position. For a quadratic potential the force is linear, so those two operations agree. For a nonlinear force, the spread and shape of the distribution can matter.

Minus V′ is force. Derivatives here are of the means in time. Ĥ, Â: Hamiltonian and observable (J; observable-dependent). The commutator expectation formula needs compatible domains and no explicit time dependence of Â. steps: For a free particle with m=2.0×10⁻³⁰ kg and ⟨p⟩=6.0×10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s, the mean-position rate is 3.0×10⁵ m/s. In 2.0×10⁻¹⁵ s its mean shifts by 6.0×10⁻¹⁰ m.

The force evaluated at ⟨x⟩ would instead be −4α(1 m)³=−8 N. These supplied moments illustrate why replacing an average of a nonlinear expression can fail.

lessons.title: Spread belongs to a preparation and a measurement
lessons.idea: Prepare the same state repeatedly. Measure position on one set of copies and momentum on another. Their probability distributions have their own means and standard deviations.
body: Prepare the same state repeatedly. Measure position on one set of copies and momentum on another. Their probability distributions have their own means and standard deviations.

For a finite distribution, standard deviation is the square root of the mean squared distance from the mean. A coarse position measurement that reports two bins can illustrate this arithmetic, but its bin labels do not by themselves give the exact continuous position spread.

The symbols σ_x and σ_p refer to the actual position and momentum distributions of a state. They are not automatically the resolution of a detector, and they are not two sharp values hidden inside this calculation.

Angle brackets denote a probability-weighted average. x, p: position and momentum outcomes (m; kg·m/s). The continuous distributions, not an arbitrary pairing of samples, define the spreads. steps: For arithmetic practice, let a coarse position device report −2 nm and +2 nm with equal probabilities. Its reported-value mean is zero and its reported-value standard deviation is 2 nm.
Change those probabilities to 3/4 and 1/4. The reported mean is −1 nm; the variance is 3 nm², giving √3 nm≈1.73205 nm.
These are statistics of the stated two-bin readout. They are not yet an exact wavefunction’s σ_x, and no σ_p was supplied.

lessons.title: A narrow Gaussian has a broad momentum distribution
lessons.idea: Choose the normalized whole-line Gaussian ψ(x)=(2πσ²)^(−1/4) exp[−(x−x₀)²/(4σ²)] exp[ip₀(x−x₀)/ℏ]. Its position density is a Gaussian centred at x₀ with standard deviation σ. The final phase factor gives mean momentum p₀ without changing that density.
body: Choose the normalized whole-line Gaussian ψ(x)=(2πσ²)^(−1/4) exp[−(x−x₀)²/(4σ²)] exp[ip₀(x−x₀)/ℏ]. Its position density is a Gaussian centred at x₀ with standard deviation σ. The final phase factor gives mean momentum p₀ without changing that density.

Define the momentum amplitude by φ(p)=(2πℏ)^(−1/2)∫exp(−ipx/ℏ)ψ(x)dx. The inverse uses exp(+ipx/ℏ). With this convention, both ∫|ψ|²dx and ∫|φ|²dp equal one. φ has units of inverse square root of momentum, not inverse square root of length.

Substitute the Gaussian and combine the linear phase terms. The Gaussian integral gives φ(p)=[2σ²/(πℏ²)]^(1/4) exp[−σ²(p−p₀)²/ℏ²] exp(−ipx₀/ℏ). Squaring its magnitude removes the last phase. Comparing the resulting exponent with a normal probability density gives σ_p=ℏ/(2σ), so σ_xσ_p=ℏ/2.

Their squared magnitudes are densities in their own variables. x, p, dx: position, momentum and position element (m; kg·m/s; m). The integral adds over the whole real line; px/ℏ is dimensionless. σ_x, σ_p: standard deviations (m; kg·m/s). Changing x₀ or p₀ shifts means without changing these widths. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

lessons.title: An overlap inequality limits two spreads
lessons.idea: Cauchy–Schwarz says that squared overlap cannot exceed the product of squared lengths: |⟨u,v⟩|²≤⟨u,u⟩⟨v,v⟩. The norm ||u|| is √⟨u,u⟩. For real columns u=(1,2) and v=(2,0), overlap is 2, so 4≤5×4=20. This geometric inequality also works for complex state vectors.
body: Cauchy–Schwarz says that squared overlap cannot exceed the product of squared lengths: |⟨u,v⟩|²≤⟨u,u⟩⟨v,v⟩. The norm ||u|| is √⟨u,u⟩. For real columns u=(1,2) and v=(2,0), overlap is 2, so 4≤5×4=20. This geometric inequality also works for complex state vectors.

For a normalized state ψ, form u=(Â−⟨A⟩)ψ and v=(B̂−⟨B⟩)ψ. Their squared norms are σ_A² and σ_B². Thus σ_Aσ_B≥|⟨u,v⟩|. The magnitude of a complex number is at least the magnitude of its imaginary part.

For self-adjoint observables with compatible products, that imaginary part is ⟨[Â,B̂]⟩/(2i). Taking magnitudes gives the Robertson bound below. For canonical position and momentum on suitable states, the commutator expectation is iℏ and the bound becomes ℏ/2.

Â, B̂, σ_A, σ_B: observables and their spreads (observable-specific). The product of spread units matches the commutator unit. [Â,B̂], ψ: commutator and normalized state (product operator unit; state amplitude). Both successive operator actions and finite variances are required. ½, | |: one half and magnitude (dimensionless operations). For a complex expectation take its complex magnitude, not its real part alone. lessons.idea: Preparation spread, detector resolution and disturbance during measurement are different questions. The uncertainty bound already constrains the state before you choose a detector.

For the unchirped Gaussian with zero mean momentum, ⟨p²⟩=σ_p². A free particle’s mean kinetic energy is ⟨K⟩=⟨p²⟩/(2m)=ℏ²/(8mσ_x²). Making this preparation narrower raises its mean kinetic energy.

This comparison does not explain how the state was prepared. An apparatus that changes the state must account for energy transfers. It does not show energy appearing from nothing, energy being borrowed, or consciousness controlling outcomes.

lessons.title: Energy sets the local shape rule
lessons.idea: A stationary spatial function obeys a second-derivative equation. The sign of V−E determines whether a constant-potential region supports sinusoidal or exponential solutions.
body: A stationary spatial function obeys a second-derivative equation. The sign of V−E determines whether a constant-potential region supports sinusoidal or exponential solutions.

If E>V, write k=√[2m(E−V)]/ℏ. The equation is φ″=−k²φ, with sine and cosine or complex travelling-wave solutions. If E<V, write κ=√[2m(V−E)]/ℏ. Then φ″=κ²φ, with growing and decaying exponentials. The full boundary problem decides which combination is allowed.

At E=V in a constant region, φ″=0, so the local solution is a straight-line function. None of these equations makes |φ|² negative. A classically forbidden region means the classical kinetic-energy expression E−V is negative, not that probability is negative.

Use the k formula only for E>V and κ only for E<V. k, κ: oscillation wave number and positive decay constant (m⁻¹). A decaying branch exp(−κx) falls toward increasing x. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. lessons.title: A finite step does not tear the amplitude
lessons.idea: At a finite bounded potential step, join the solutions from the two sides. For constant mass and an ordinary finite-energy state, both the amplitude and its first derivative are continuous.
body: At a finite bounded potential step, join the solutions from the two sides. For constant mass and an ordinary finite-energy state, both the amplitude and its first derivative are continuous.

Integrate the stationary equation across an interval shrinking onto the step. The integral of bounded (V−E)φ goes to zero, so the derivative change φ′(a+)−φ′(a−) goes to zero. A jump in φ itself would create singular derivatives not balanced by a bounded potential; the allowed amplitude is continuous too.

These statements do not apply unchanged to every wall. A delta-function potential can make the first derivative jump. An ideal infinite wall imposes its own endpoint condition instead of being treated as a bounded step.

lessons.title: Symmetry can halve a boundary calculation
lessons.idea: An even potential has V(−x)=V(x). Reflecting a stationary solution then gives another solution at the same energy. Parity names the reflection rule: an even amplitude stays the same, while an odd amplitude changes sign.
body: An even potential has V(−x)=V(x). Reflecting a stationary solution then gives another solution at the same energy. Parity names the reflection rule: an even amplitude stays the same, while an odd amplitude changes sign.

For a regular confining one-dimensional scalar problem on the line, with the usual self-adjoint domain and decaying bound-state boundary data, a discrete bound energy is nondegenerate: there is only one independent eigenfunction up to a constant factor. One reason is that the Wronskian of two same-energy solutions is constant; decay makes it zero, forcing dependence.

Reflection must therefore return a constant times the same bound eigenfunction. Reflect twice to get back the original, so the factor is +1 or −1. An even differentiable function has φ′(0)=0; an odd one has φ(0)=0. These centre conditions simplify a calculation, but the distant decay condition must still be satisfied.

At x=L, |g|²=|C|² exp(−1)≈0.367879|C|². These parity tests alone do not establish either trial shape as an eigenfunction of an arbitrary potential.

lessons.title: Try an energy, then check the far boundary
lessons.idea: Shooting means starting a differential equation at one end, integrating a trial solution, and checking how far it misses the other end. The miss is a residual. A small residual is a numerical check, not a guarantee that every eigenvalue was found.
body: Shooting means starting a differential equation at one end, integrating a trial solution, and checking how far it misses the other end. The miss is a residual. A small residual is a numerical check, not a guarantee that every eigenvalue was found.

Use a confined segment 0<x<L with zero amplitude at both endpoints and V=0 inside. Set s=x/L and ε=E/E₀, where E₀=ℏ²/(2mL²). Write φ=C u(s), so u is dimensionless and obeys u″=−εu. Here primes mean derivatives with respect to s. Start u(0)=0 and u′(0)=1; the arbitrary slope fixes scale before normalization.

For each trial ε, integrate to s=1 and record R(ε)=u(1). A bracket is two trial energies with residuals of opposite signs. For a continuous residual, a root lies between them. Bisection tests the midpoint, keeps the half with opposite endpoint signs, and repeats. A sign change brackets some root, not necessarily every root.

Our numerical integration uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta on u′=w and w′=−εu: within each equal step it combines the initial slope, two midpoint slope estimates and an endpoint estimate with weights 1, 2, 2, 1 divided by 6. Step refinement means repeating with smaller steps. Compare both the root and residual; a tiny bisection bracket cannot repair a poorly integrated differential equation.

C supplies φ’s amplitude units; normalize the final shape separately. ε, R: scaled trial energy and residual (dimensionless). R tests the endpoint u(1)=0. E, E₀, L, m: energy, energy scale, segment length and mass (J; J; m; kg). The endpoints impose ideal zero-amplitude conditions, not finite-step derivative continuity. N, Δs: number of integration steps and step length (dimensionless). Use N equal steps of size Δs=1/N; smaller Δs tests discretization. Numerical substitutions use the stated units. m is metre, s second, kg kilogram, J joule, N newton and rad radian. nm means 10⁻⁹ m. i²=−1; * means complex conjugate; |z|² means z* z. π is the circle constant. When needed, use rounded ℏ=1.054571817×10⁻³⁴ J·s; ℏ=h/(2π), not h. Square roots denote the nonnegative root.

example.title: Work through one case
steps: The exact reference for this test equation is u(s)=sin(√ε s)/√ε for ε>0. Thus R(8)≈+0.108920 and R(12)≈−0.091495; [8,12] brackets the first positive root.

Bisection with Runge–Kutta integration gives ε≈9.869610646 for N=40, and approximately 9.869604792 for N=80. Both approach the reference π²≈9.869604401 as steps shrink. At N=160 the root is approximately 9.869604426. The integrated endpoint residual at each computed root is below 2×10⁻¹⁵, yet the energy error still falls with step refinement. Rounded display digits are not solver tolerances.

For L=1.0 nm and m=2.0×10⁻³⁰ kg, E₀≈2.78030×10⁻²¹ J. The first root corresponds to E≈2.74405×10⁻²⁰ J. Normalizing the converged spatial shape is a separate step; the initial slope 1 was only a scale choice.

lessons.title: Walls select allowed wavelengths
lessons.idea: Only sine patterns that vanish at both walls are allowed stationary states.
body: Consider a particle of positive mass m on 0<x<L. Set potential energy to zero inside and impose ψ(0)=ψ(L)=0 at ideal impenetrable walls. These boundary values are part of the model, not ordinary matching through a finite step.

For positive energy, the stationary equation gives ψ=A sin(kx)+B cos(kx), with k²=2mE/ℏ². The left wall sets B=0. The right wall requires sin(kL)=0, so kL=nπ. Positive integers n=1,2,… give distinct states. The n=0 sine is zero everywhere and cannot be normalized; solving E=0 directly also gives only the zero function with these boundaries.

Normalizing each allowed sine gives the eigenfunction below. The energies grow as n². An energy eigenfunction acquires a common time phase, but its position density stays fixed. It is not a little particle bouncing along a drawn sine curve.

lessons.title: A zero mean is not zero kinetic energy
lessons.idea: Spread and mean-square motion remain nonzero even when a signed mean vanishes.
body: For a normalized well eigenstate, the density is symmetric about L/2, so the position mean is L/2. The standard deviation measures spread around that mean, not the range of possible outcomes. Integrating x² against the sine-squared density gives ⟨x²⟩=L²[1/3−1/(2n²π²)]. Subtracting ⟨x⟩² gives the variance below.

The formal first-derivative integral ∫ψ* (−iℏ dψ/dx)dx is zero for these real sine states. Yet ∫ℏ²|dψ/dx|²dx=(nπℏ/L)² is positive, so kinetic energy is positive. Opposite momentum contributions can have zero mean without zero mean square.

The confined Hamiltonian is well defined with zero endpoint values. The first-derivative momentum expression with those same endpoint conditions is not by itself a self-adjoint momentum observable. If we discuss a momentum distribution after ideal sudden release, the zero-extended sine state has the quoted mean and second moment. Do not silently treat the confined momentum operator as self-adjoint.

lessons.title: Relative phase changes a region probability
lessons.idea: A relative phase can move probability between regions without changing energy populations.
body: Prepare equal real amplitudes of the first two well energy states at t=0. Orthogonality makes Ψ=(ψ₁e^(−iE₁t/ℏ)+ψ₂e^(−iE₂t/ℏ))/√2 normalized at every time. The two phases run at different rates, so their interference can change position probabilities even though energy probabilities stay one half each.

For the left half, each individual state contributes probability one half. The cross integral is ∫₀ᴸ⧸₂ψ₁ψ₂dx=4/(3π). One way to evaluate it is sin u sin2u=[cos u−cos3u]/2, integrated from u=0 to π/2. This gives P_left=1/2+[4/(3π)]cos[(E₂−E₁)t/ℏ].

The interference repeats after τ=2πℏ/(E₂−E₁). This is a probability-pattern timescale, not a travel time of a particle between walls. A common phase multiplying both components would not change any probability.

lessons.title: A ring joins the ends instead of closing them
lessons.idea: Periodic boundaries allow a constant state and pairs with opposite circulation.
body: Let s measure distance around a ring of circumference C. A physical state must return to the same value and derivative after one turn: ψ(s+C)=ψ(s) and ψ′(s+C)=ψ′(s). These are periodic boundary conditions, not zero values at two walls.

If the radius is R=C/(2π) and angle is φ=s/R, the phase is nφ. The integer n counts whole phase turns. A one-dimensional bound-state nondegeneracy argument based on decay at infinity does not cover this periodic domain.

lessons.title: A finite well has oscillations and tails
lessons.idea: Finite confinement permits decaying amplitude outside, but matching still chooses the energy.
body: Choose the potential zero at the bottom: V(x)=0 for |x|<a and V(x)=V₀ outside. Here V₀>0 and the width is 2a. A bound state has 0<E<V₀ with this reference. Shifting every potential and energy by the same constant would not change the shape.

Inside, the stationary equation gives oscillations with k=√(2mE)/ℏ. Outside it gives exponentials with κ=√[2m(V₀−E)]/ℏ. Normalizability selects decay on both sides: exp[−κ(x−a)] on the right and exp[κ(x+a)] on the left. Growing tails are rejected for a bound state extending over the whole line.

Even states can use cos(kx) inside; odd states use sin(kx). The allowed energy still needs matching at both edges. Writing a locally valid oscillation and a tail at an arbitrary energy is not yet an eigenstate.

body: At a finite step with constant mass and no delta singularity, both ψ and its first derivative are continuous. For an even state write A cos(kx) inside and A cos(ka)exp[−κ(x−a)] for x≥a. At x=a, derivative matching gives −Ak sin(ka)=−κA cos(ka), hence k tan(ka)=κ.

lessons.idea: A numerical root must satisfy the equation and its physical interval.
body: A bracket is an interval whose continuous residual has opposite signs at its ends. For the even equation use F(z)=z tan z−√(z₀²−z²). Bisection evaluates the midpoint and keeps the half that still brackets zero. It reduces the bracket width without assuming the graph is straight.

For depth z₀=2, the interval [1,1.1] stays inside the first tangent branch and inside the allowed energy range. Repeated halving gives z≈1.02986653. Substituting back checks the matching residual as well as the allowed interval. A small printed residual and a small bracket describe numerical accuracy, not experimental uncertainty.

There is also one odd root in (π/2,2), about 1.89549427. No later positive matching branch begins below z₀=2, so this well has exactly two bound states. More generally each allowed branch must be checked; a state exactly at the outside threshold is not counted as normalizable. For very shallow positive depth there is still an even bound state, with a long tail.

body: Use the lowest even matched state. Inside |x|<a let ψ=A cos(kx); outside let ψ=A cos(ka)exp[−κ(|x|−a)]. Both tails are present. Choose A positive and real; its sign would only change a global phase.

Nonzero outside density means a position detection can occur where E<V₀. It does not describe a particle borrowing energy or repeatedly escaping from this stationary state. A real bound eigenfunction has zero probability current even with nonzero tails.

lessons.idea: Compare outgoing probability currents, including their different speeds.
body: For left incidence on a real time-independent potential, write the left asymptotic wave as A exp(ik_Lx)+B exp(−ik_Lx), and the right as C exp(ik_Rx). Both k values are positive and the same particle mass is used on both sides. These stationary plane waves are generalized scattering states, not normalized over the whole line.

The current j=(ℏ/m)Im(ψ* dψ/dx) gives positive incident flow, negative reflected flow and positive transmitted flow. Define R as the magnitude of reflected current divided by incident current, and T as transmitted current divided by incident current. The different velocities produce the factor k_R/k_L in T.

For a lossless stationary setup with no other open channels, R+T=1. This is a current balance. |C|² alone is neither a whole-space probability nor generally the transmission fraction. Finite normalized packets provide the later measurement interpretation.

lessons.title: An upward step can reflect above its height
lessons.idea: Matching value and slope predicts partial reflection even above a finite step.
body: Let V=0 for x<0 and V=V₀>0 for x>0, with E>V₀. Choose incident amplitude one in relative units and write ψ_left∝exp(ik₁x)+r exp(−ik₁x), ψ_right∝t exp(ik₂x). Here k₁=√(2mE)/ℏ and k₂=√[2m(E−V₀)]/ℏ.

At the finite step, matching the value gives 1+r=t. Matching the derivative gives k₁(1−r)=k₂t. Solving yields r=(k₁−k₂)/(k₁+k₂) and t=2k₁/(k₁+k₂). Even with enough energy to propagate on the right, mismatched wave numbers can cause reflection.
Convert amplitudes to currents: R=r² and T=4k₁k₂/(k₁+k₂)². Their sum is one. As V₀ tends to zero at fixed positive E, the wave numbers match and reflection vanishes.

lessons.title: A packet turns flux fractions into detection chances
lessons.idea: A normalized packet averages the stationary transmission over its energy distribution.
body: A physical incident state can be a normalized packet rather than an infinite plane wave. Far before the encounter, prepare it on the left with mostly positive momenta. Far afterwards, if reflected and transmitted parts have separated and no probability remains trapped, integrate their densities over their separate regions.

For a narrow energy distribution centred at E₀ where T(E) varies little, the transmitted probability is approximately T(E₀). More generally P_trans=∫w(E)T(E)dE, where w(E) is the normalized incident energy probability density. Its units are inverse energy, so the integral is dimensionless.

For a real time-independent barrier, each energy component keeps the same total energy. The two outgoing probabilities sum to one under the stated completeness conditions. This account describes preparation and later detections; it does not supply a unique hidden path or one universal tunnelling time.

body: For the one-dimensional oscillator, V(x)=mω²x²/2 with positive mass m and angular frequency ω. The Hamiltonian is H=−(ℏ²/2m)d²/dx²+mω²x²/2 on the whole line. Its two parts are kinetic and potential energy, not two independent state probabilities.

ℓ is not the ground-state position standard deviation. The normalized ground density will give Δx=ℓ/√2. Calling every width simply “the oscillator length” would lose this factor.

lessons.title: Operators move between normalized levels
lessons.idea: Raising and lowering relate levels, but operator order changes the result.
body: Let D=d/dξ. Define the lowering operator a=(ξ+D)/√2 and raising operator a†=(ξ−D)/√2. The dagger means the adjoint on the appropriate oscillator domain; it is not ordinary complex conjugation of a number. Products act on the state to their right, with the rightmost operator applied first.

The product rule gives [D,ξ]f=D(ξf)−ξDf=f. Consequently [a,a†]=1 and H=ℏω(a†a+1/2) on a shared suitable domain. One safe working domain is finite linear combinations of oscillator eigenfunctions, where all these actions remain defined.

Write |n⟩ for a normalized oscillator energy state, n=0,1,…. Then a|n⟩=√n|n−1⟩ and a†|n⟩=√(n+1)|n+1⟩. The lowering action on |0⟩ is zero, not a state with negative label. These coefficients preserve the normalization bookkeeping; applying an operator is not automatically an outcome probability.
lessons.terms: a, a†, D, ξ: lowering, raising, derivative operator and scaled position (dimensionless operators; none). D differentiates with respect to ξ; brackets mean AB−BA. |n⟩, n: normalized number state and level label (abstract state; none). The position representation has units m⁻¹ᐟ². H, Eₙ, ω: Hamiltonian, level energy and angular frequency (J operator; J; rad/s). The numeral 1 in a commutator means the identity action. Units and notation: m as a unit means metre; nm is 10⁻⁹ m, s second, kg kilogram, J joule and eV electronvolt. A particle mass also uses the letter m, as defined above. ℏ=h/(2π), with h the Planck constant; use rounded ℏ=1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s or 0.6582 eV·fs only when stated, and 1 fs=10⁻¹⁵ s. π≈3.14159 and e≈2.71828. i²=−1. An integral adds contributions; d/dx differentiates with respect to x. A star conjugates a complex number; | | is magnitude; squared magnitude is nonnegative. Bare substitutions use the stated units. In one dimension a normalized wavefunction has units length⁻¹ᐟ² and its squared magnitude has units length⁻¹.

lessons.title: Calculate distributions, not imagined orbits
lessons.idea: A superposition can change means while energy remains a distribution of allowed levels.
body: For a number state |n⟩, ladder orthogonality gives ⟨x⟩=⟨p⟩=0, ⟨x²⟩=ℓ²(n+1/2) and ⟨p²⟩=(ℏ²/ℓ²)(n+1/2). Use x=ℓ(a+a†)/√2 and p=ℏ(a−a†)/(i√2ℓ). Only terms that return to the same level contribute to a number-state expectation.

Now prepare (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2 with real equal coefficients at time zero. The cross term gives ⟨x⟩=ℓ/√2 and ⟨p⟩=0. Meanwhile ⟨x²⟩=ℓ² and ⟨p²⟩=ℏ²/ℓ². Subtracting the squared means gives (Δx)²=ℓ²/2 and (Δp)²=ℏ²/ℓ².

An energy measurement on that superposition gives ℏω/2 or 3ℏω/2 with probability one half each. Its mean energy ℏω is not a third possible outcome in this preparation. This two-level state is not a coherent state, the distinct family whose full expansion contains infinitely many number levels except the vacuum case.

lessons.title: Describe the same state using momentum
lessons.idea: Position and momentum representations are two descriptions of one state, not two independent states.
body: Use φ(p)=(2πℏ)^(−1/2)∫ exp(−ipx/ℏ)ψ(x)dx. This Fourier convention changes a position wavefunction into a momentum wavefunction. The inverse uses exp(+ipx/ℏ) and integrates over p with the same prefactor. The symbol φ here is a wavefunction, not a phase angle.

Both representations are normalized:∫|ψ|²dx=∫|φ|²dp=1. This norm-preserving Fourier property is Parseval’s identity for the stated convention. Since dp has momentum units, φ has units(kg·m/s)⁻¹ᐟ², not the inverse-square-root-length units of ψ.

The momentum mean is⟨p⟩=∫p|φ(p)|²dp. Probability comes from integrating the spectral density over a momentum interval. A peak in that density does not make every individual momentum measurement equal to the peak value.

The angle brackets mean an ensemble expectation, not one result. steps: Take a normalized momentum amplitude that is constant in magnitude for p₀−P≤p≤p₀+P and zero outside, with P>0. Its magnitude is 1/√(2P), so density is 1/(2P).

The mean is the midpoint p₀. The probability between 2.5×10⁻²⁴ and 3.5×10⁻²⁴ kg·m/s is one half. This sharp spectral-window example has long position tails; it is not a Gaussian-width example.

lessons.title: A free packet can spread while its centre moves steadily
lessons.idea: Spreading is a change in the distribution’s width, not necessarily acceleration of its centre.
body: Start from an unchirped Gaussian with centre x₀, position standard deviation σ₀>0 and mean momentum p₀. Unchirped means no initial quadratic position-dependent phase. Its free evolution uses H=p̂²/(2m), with no potential and no interactions.

Define τ=ℏt/(2mσ₀²) and q=1+iτ. The exact solution can be written ψ=Nq^(−1/2)exp[−(x−x_c)²/(4σ₀²q)]exp[i p₀(x−x₀)/ℏ−i p₀²t/(2mℏ)], where N=(2πσ₀²)^(−1/4) and x_c=x₀+p₀t/m. Choose the square-root branch continuously from q=1 at t=0. The last exponential changes phase; its magnitude is one.

Taking the squared magnitude uses|q|=√(1+τ²). The resulting density is Gaussian with centre x_c and width σ_x(t)=σ₀√(1+τ²). The momentum width remains σ_p=ℏ/(2σ₀), because free momentum probabilities do not change. The time t_s=2mσ₀²/ℏ is the scale where the position width grows by √2.

The phase factors and shifting centre satisfy the free Schrödinger equation. The density integrates to one at every time. This is an ensemble position distribution; it is not a movie of one particle expanding into a material cloud.

lessons.title: Compare time and length scales before using a classical picture
lessons.idea: A small quantum correction in one calculation does not make every quantum feature disappear.
body: For the free Gaussian, the dimensionless spreading parameter is τ=ℏt/(2mσ₀²). If|τ|≪1, then σ_x(t)/σ₀=√(1+τ²)≈1+τ²/2. The approximation comes from expanding the square root near zero. It controls this width change, not every possible quantum effect.

Mean motion can also look classical: Ehrenfest’s equation gives d⟨p⟩/dt=−⟨V′(x)⟩. Replacing the mean force by−V′(⟨x⟩) needs the force to vary little across the occupied packet, or a force exactly linear in x. A small spreading parameter alone does not justify that separate replacement.

Even when the mean follows a classical equation, the state still predicts a distribution of outcomes. Coherence, interference and correlations depend on preparation and the environment as well as mass. Do not use “large mass” or “short wavelength” as a universal rule erasing quantum structure.

Packet width and the force’s variation scale matter. The exact equality for a linear spring is a special case, not a universal identity.

lessons.title: Describe a point by distance and two angles
lessons.idea: Spherical coordinates are useful when the interaction depends only on distance from the centre.
body: Let r be distance from the origin, θ the polar angle measured from positive z, and φ the azimuth measured in the x-y plane from positive x toward positive y. The ranges are r≥0,0≤θ≤π and 0≤φ<2π. The symbols θ and φ name different angles.

The Cartesian coordinates are x=r sinθcosφ, y=r sinθsinφ and z=r cosθ. A tiny spherical cell has approximate side lengths dr, r dθ and r sinθ dφ. Multiplying them gives the volume element dV=r²sinθ dr dθ dφ. The angles are in radians; their differentials are dimensionless in SI dimensional algebra.

The solid-angle element dΩ=sinθ dθ dφ sums to 4π over every direction. Integrating the volume element between radii a and b gives 4π(b³−a³)/3. Azimuth is not uniquely defined on the polar axis, and all angles are ambiguous at r=0; those coordinate singularities do not mean the physical space has a hole.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why can a radial probability integral not usually omit the r² factor?
apply.answer: A shell farther from the centre contains more spatial volume for the same radial thickness. The probability in that shell must include its volume measure. Omitting r² would generally confuse density per volume with probability per radial distance.

lessons.title: A shell probability is different from density at a point
lessons.idea: A larger shell can contain more probability even when density per volume is constant.
body: In three dimensions, probability is∫|ψ(r)|²dV. The normalized wavefunction has units m⁻³ᐟ² and the density has units m⁻³. These differ from the one-dimensional units because the integration measure is volume.

For a spherically symmetric state, density depends only on r. Integrating over directions gives the radial probability density P_r(r)=4πr²|ψ(r)|². Then probability between radii a andb is∫ₐᵇP_r(r)dr. P_r has units m⁻¹ and is not the same function as the volume density.

For a simple probability example, take constant amplitude A inside a ball of radius R and zero outside. Normalization gives|A|²[4πR³/3]=1, so radial density inside is 3r²/R³. This sharp boundary is a probability example only; it is not automatically a finite-kinetic-energy or stationary state for an ordinary smooth Hamiltonian.
