lessons.title: Measure one component of orbital angular momentum
lessons.idea: Rotation around one axis is described by how the state changes with the azimuth angle.
body: For a scalar position wavefunction, the orbital z-component operator is L̂_z=−iℏ∂/∂φ. It acts on the azimuth coordinate φ, not on the radial distance. Orbital refers to spatial rotation properties; this is distinct from intrinsic spin.
An azimuthal factor Φ_m(φ)=e^(imφ)/√(2π) is an eigenfunction because differentiating gives∂Φ_m/∂φ=imΦ_m, and then L̂_zΦ_m=mℏΦ_m. The integer label m is a quantum number here, not mass.

Single-valued orbital scalar states must return to the same value after φ increases by 2π. Since e^(i2πm)=1, this azimuthal label is an integer. The factorΦ_m is normalized overφ, but it is only an angular factor, not by itself a complete admissible three-dimensional wavefunction at the polar axes.

lessons.title: Total orbital size and one component can be definite together
lessons.idea: Angular-momentum components are not three simultaneously sharp classical numbers.
body: Orbital operators obey[L̂_x,L̂_y]=iℏL̂_z and cyclic counterparts. The total square L̂²=L̂_x²+L̂_y²+L̂_z² commutes with L̂_z. That permits common eigenstates with L² eigenvalueℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1) and L_z eigenvalue mℏ.

For scalar orbital states, ℓ is a nonnegative integer and m runs through−ℓ,−ℓ+1,…,ℓ. The square-root scale√[ℓ(ℓ+1)]ℏ is the magnitude associated with L², not the same number as a measured z-component. Do not draw it as a classical vector with all components simultaneously known.

Angular wavefunctions are normalized with dΩ=sinθdθdφ. The simplest is Y₀₀=1/√(4π), which is constant over direction and hasℓ=m=0. Another is Y₁₀=√(3/(4π))cosθ. Its azimuthal derivative is zero, so m=0, while its total-angular-momentum square is 2ℏ².

To verify the last statement, the spherical angular operator is L̂²=−ℏ²[(1/sinθ)∂_θ(sinθ∂_θ)+(1/sin²θ)∂_φ²]. Acting on Ccosθ gives 2ℏ²Ccosθ: theφ derivative vanishes, and theθ derivatives produce−2Ccosθ inside the brackets. C is the stated normalization coefficient.

lessons.title: Separate angular shape from radial behavior
lessons.idea: For a central potential, angular labels turn part of the problem into an effective radial equation.
body: A central potential depends only on r, so write a stationary state as ψ(r,θ,φ)=R(r)Y_ℓm(θ,φ). Normalize Y over solid angle. Then the radial normalization is∫₀∞|R|²r²dr=1, without an extra 4π because Y already accounts for the directions.

The spherical Laplacian can be written∇²=(1/r²)∂_r(r²∂_r)−L̂²/(ℏ²r²). It is the 3D second-derivative operator expressed in spherical coordinates. Substituting the separated state into the stationary Schrödinger equation replaces L̂² by its eigenvalueℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1).

Set u(r)=rR(r). The first-derivative radial terms simplify, giving−(ℏ²/(2μ))u″+[V(r)+ℏ²ℓ(ℓ+1)/(2μr²)]u=Eu. Here μ is the particle or reduced mass, and a prime means derivative with respect to r. The radial norm becomes∫₀∞|u|²dr=1.

The extra positive term for ℓ>0 is the centrifugal contribution to the effective potential. This is a term in a wave equation, not proof of a classical orbit. The domain is r≥0, with a boundary condition at the origin; it is not the entire one-dimensional x axis.

apply.text: How does this relate to P_r=4πr²|ψ|² for a spherical state?

lessons.title: Check the origin as well as the far tail
lessons.idea: A radial solution must be admissible at both ends of a half-line.
body: For potentials regular at the origin, or Coulomb-like 1/r behavior without a point interaction, the regular radial solution behaves as u∝r^(ℓ+1) near r=0. The other local power behaves as r^(−ℓ) and is excluded by the regular 3D domain. These leading powers come from balancing the centrifugal and second-derivative terms.

For ℓ=0 the excluded branch can approach a constant u, which would make R=u/r singular. Square-integrability alone is not the whole domain test: a1/r singularity can be locally integrable in volume but fail the stated regular Hamiltonian conditions. Here use u(0)=0.

For a bound state with V(r)→0 at large r and E<0, the leading decay scale is κ=√(−2μE)/ℏ. An exponentially growing branch is not normalizable. The far solution has a decaying exponential e^(−κr); long-range Coulomb potentials can also supply a multiplying power of r, so this statement identifies the leading exponential rather than every prefactor.

lessons.title: Both members of an atom can move
lessons.idea: A proton is much heavier than an electron, but it is not infinitely heavy.
body: Let r⃗=r⃗_e−r⃗_p point from proton to electron. Its length r is their separation. The centre of mass is R⃗=(m_e r⃗_e+m_p r⃗_p)/(m_e+m_p). These two coordinates separate overall motion from motion inside the atom. An orbital wavefunction describes the relative coordinate; it is not an electron track around a fixed point.

Write M=m_e+m_p and μ=m_e m_p/M. The kinetic energy separates into P²/(2M)+p²/(2μ), where P is total momentum and p is conjugate to the relative coordinate. “Conjugate” here means the momentum paired with that coordinate in the Hamiltonian. The interaction depends only on r: V(r)=−k_e e²/r. Thus the internal wavefunction uses the reduced mass μ, not M.

Two useful scales follow from the internal radial equation. Set a=ℏ²/(μ k_e e²) and E_R=ℏ²/(2μa²). With ρ=r/a, the radial equation becomes [−d²/dρ²+ℓ(ℓ+1)/ρ²−2/ρ]u=(E/E_R)u. The coefficient 2 in the attraction follows because k_e e²/a=2E_R. This is a balance of equation coefficients, not an assumption of a circular orbit.

Taking the proton mass as infinite would set μ=m_e. A finite proton makes μ slightly smaller, a slightly larger and E_R slightly smaller. The following small examples use rounded hydrogen scales a≈0.0529 nm and E_R≈13.6 eV; these do not resolve fine or hyperfine spectral structure.
lessons.terms: m_e, m_p, M, μ: Electron mass, proton mass, total mass and reduced mass (kg). All masses are positive. μ is used for relative motion; M is used for overall centre-of-mass motion. r⃗_e, r⃗_p, r⃗, R⃗, r, a, ρ: Positions, relative and centre coordinates, separation, Coulomb length scale and scaled radius (m except dimensionless ρ). ρ=r/a. A vector arrow marks a direction as well as a size; r is nonnegative. P, p: Centre-of-mass and relative momentum magnitudes (kg·m/s). P²/(2M) and p²/(2μ) are separate kinetic-energy terms. k_e, e, ℏ: Coulomb constant, positive elementary charge and reduced Planck constant (N·m²/C², C, J·s). Electron charge is −e; proton charge is +e, giving the attractive negative potential. In the scaled equation d²/dρ² differentiates with respect to the unit-free radius. lessons.idea: The most likely radius and the largest density at one point are different questions.
body: For the lowest Coulomb state, ψ_1s(r)=exp(−r/a)/√(πa³). It has no angle dependence. Since Y₀₀=1/√(4π), its radial factors are R(r)=2a^(−3/2)exp(−r/a) and u(r)=rR(r). The label 1s means n=1 and ℓ=0; it is not a path.

Check the radial equation using u=C r exp(−r/a). For r>0, u″/u=1/a²−2/(ar). Substitution into −ℏ²u″/(2μ)−k_e e²u/r=Eu cancels the 1/r terms because ℏ²/(μa)=k_e e². The remaining energy is E=−ℏ²/(2μa²)=−E_R. The solution also has u(0)=0 and decays at large r.
Normalization uses volume, not just dr: ∫₀∞4πr²|ψ|²dr=(4/a³)∫₀∞r²e^(−2r/a)dr=1. The final integral is a³/4, obtainable by two integrations by parts. The radial density is P_r(r)=4r²e^(−2r/a)/a³.

The volume density |ψ|² decreases from its largest value at r=0. The radial density instead vanishes at r=0 and peaks at r=a: its derivative has the sign of 1−r/a for r>0. A shell farther out contains more volume, which changes the question. The probability at any exact point, or exact radius, is zero in this continuous distribution.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Why can a density be nonzero at the origin while the radial density is zero there?
apply.answer: The two densities use different volume measures. A very thin shell has volume about 4πr²dr, which shrinks toward zero near the origin. Multiplying volume density by that shell factor gives radial density. Neither density height is the probability of a single exact point.

lessons.title: Use the allowed energy labels without turning them into orbits
lessons.idea: The bound-state energy labels come from acceptable wavefunctions and their boundaries.
body: The nonrelativistic Coulomb bound energies are E_n=−E_R/n² for n=1,2,3,… . The positive integer n labels a family of acceptable states. For each n, the orbital label ℓ runs from 0 to n−1, and the component label m runs in integer steps from −ℓ to +ℓ.

Why integers? After factoring out the required regular-origin behavior and decaying tail, the radial differential equation gives a power-series recurrence. For a bound state, the remaining series must stop at a nonnegative integer degree; otherwise the resulting solution grows too much at large radius. This supplies the allowed relation n=n_r+ℓ+1, where n_r is that radial degree. We state this general result and verify low states in this course; the full recurrence proof is a separate depth extension.

In this ideal Hamiltonian, energy depends on n, not separately on ℓ or m. The number of spatial states at that energy is ∑_(ℓ=0)^(n−1)(2ℓ+1)=n². Having different states at the same energy is called degeneracy. This count excludes spin and does not survive every correction or external field.

All these bound energies are negative because zero is chosen at infinite separation with zero relative kinetic energy. As n increases they approach zero from below. Positive internal energies belong to scattering states, not to a bound level with a noninteger n.

lessons.title: Find where an excited-state amplitude vanishes
lessons.idea: A node is a zero of a wavefunction, not a wall that traps a little orbit.
body: Use the dimensionless radius ρ=r/a. Two normalized radial factors are R₂₀=(2−ρ)e^(−ρ/2)/(2√2 a^(3/2)) and R₂₁=ρe^(−ρ/2)/(2√6 a^(3/2)). The subscripts mean n and ℓ. Each obeys ∫₀∞|R|²r²dr=1. Multiplying by a normalized angular factor gives a normalized 3D state.

For 2s, combine R₂₀ with Y₀₀=1/√(4π). Its amplitude vanishes on the sphere r=2a because 2−ρ=0. This is an internal radial node. For 2p with m=0, combine R₂₁ with Y₁₀=√(3/(4π))cosθ. The factor cosθ vanishes at θ=π/2, giving an angular node in the plane z=0.

The origin and infinity are boundaries, not the internal nodes being counted here. The 2p radial factor has no zero at a finite positive r. For a real displayed factor, the sign changes across its node; probability density remains nonnegative because it is the squared magnitude.

A single zero-thickness node has zero probability measure. The useful predictions are small-region probabilities and the pattern of nearby density. These stationary amplitudes do not show particles travelling along the coloured lobes of a drawing.

lessons.title: A level change fixes a possible photon energy
lessons.idea: Energy matching is necessary for a transition, but it does not by itself make that transition allowed.
body: For a specified allowed downward change from n_i to n_f<n_i, the emitted photon energy is ΔE=E_i−E_f=E_R(1/n_f²−1/n_i²)>0. The final atomic energy is more negative, while the photon carries positive energy away.
The photon relations are f=ΔE/h and λ=hc/ΔE in vacuum. Use h in eV·s when ΔE is in eV, or convert both to joules. In the following rounded examples h≈4.136×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s and hc≈1240 eV·nm.

We are given that the 3p→2s change is allowed in the electric-dipole approximation. The letters mean ℓ=1 and ℓ=0. Energy matching alone would not establish that statement: coupling and angular selection rules also matter. Their derivation belongs to later quantum transition methods.

Neglect atomic recoil in this introductory photon-energy calculation. Finite nuclear mass enters E_R if included consistently, while relativistic, spin and radiative corrections can further shift or split lines. The rounded numbers here are not precision laboratory wavelengths.

lessons.title: Choose the model before using a formula
lessons.idea: The preparation, boundaries and requested measurement decide which calculation fits.
body: A confined normalized state uses ∫|ψ|²dx=1 on its allowed domain. A finite-outcome state uses ∑|c_j|²=1 in an orthonormal basis. These are two versions of total probability one; continuous density must be integrated, while a discrete coefficient square already gives one outcome probability.

A stationary incident scattering wave on an infinite line is different. Its constant incoming density is not integrable over the full line, so its overall normalization is not one particle spread uniformly over infinity. Compute reflected and transmitted current ratios instead. A finite normalizable incoming packet can later connect these ratios to separated outcome probabilities when it is narrow in energy and the setup permits that approximation.

Before calculating, ask: what is prepared, which Hamiltonian applies, where are the boundaries, which outcome is measured, and which units are being used? A valid equation in the wrong domain still gives the wrong answer. A pure superposition and an ensemble mixture also require different probability bookkeeping.

A model supports the predictions it actually computes. A stationary density is not a path, an evanescent tail is not a classical speed, and a completion tick is not proof that a new problem can be solved independently.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What should you do if a problem gives neither boundaries nor preparation?
apply.answer: State what is missing instead of silently choosing a favourite formula. For example, a barrier height alone does not determine transmission: the energy, width, mass and boundary setup matter. A well-posed prediction needs the relevant inputs.

lessons.limits: Choice among the specific ideal one-particle models taught here. Mixed-state and generalized-measurement theory, experimental inverse problems and arbitrary many-body systems are not completed by this checklist.

lessons.title: Combine normalization, energy and a later position check
lessons.idea: A stationary Hamiltonian can evolve a superposition into a changing position distribution.
body: Use a hard-wall well on 0<x<L. Its normalized real modes are u_n=√(2/L)sin(nπx/L), with E_n=n²E₁. Prepare ψ(x,0)=(u₁+u₂)/√2. Orthogonality makes its norm one, even though the two position amplitudes overlap.

At time t, ψ=(u₁e^(−iE₁t/ℏ)+u₂e^(−i4E₁t/ℏ))/√2. An energy measurement gives E₁ or 4E₁ with probability 1/2 each at every time. Thus ⟨E⟩=2.5E₁ and σ_E=1.5E₁; phase changes do not change those energy weights.

Let θ=(E₂−E₁)t/ℏ=3E₁t/ℏ. The position density is (u₁²+u₂²)/2+u₁u₂cosθ. Integrating the left half uses ∫₀^(L/2)u₁u₂dx=4/(3π), so P_left=1/2+[4/(3π)]cosθ. Energy probabilities stay fixed while this interval probability changes.

The beating period is t_b=2πℏ/(3E₁): after this time the relative phase returns by a full turn. The position distribution is not stationary, despite its constant mean energy. An earlier actual energy measurement would prepare one energy mode and change the later calculation.
lessons.terms: L, x, u_n, ψ: Well length, position, normalized mode and state (m, m, m⁻¹ᐟ², m⁻¹ᐟ²). Hard walls at 0 and L, with wavefunction zero there. n=1,2 labels the occupied modes. E₁, E₂, ⟨E⟩, σ_E: First/second energies, mean energy and energy standard deviation (eV or J consistently). E₂=4E₁; variance is the weighted square deviation, and standard deviation is its square root. t, t_b, θ, ℏ: Time, beating period, relative phase and reduced Planck constant (s, s, rad, energy·s). Use ℏ≈6.582×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s when E₁ is in eV. Radian phases are dimensionless in exponentials. P_left, π: Left-half probability and circle constant (no unit). The interval is 0<x<L/2; π≈3.14159. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), C coulomb (charge), V volt (joules per coulomb), rad radian (angle). nm=10⁻⁹ m; pm=10⁻¹² m. A dot multiplies units; a slash means per. Bare arithmetic uses numerical values in the stated units. Symbols for quantities are defined separately from unit labels. ℏ means h/(2π), about 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s in rounded examples. eV is an energy unit, about 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J; it is not voltage. μm=10⁻⁶ m. State any further numerical scale before using it.

example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Choose a well whose first energy is E₁=0.20 eV. The two energy outcomes are 0.20 and 0.80 eV, each with probability 1/2.
The mean is 0.50 eV and the standard deviation is 0.30 eV. With rounded ℏ=6.582×10⁻¹⁶ eV·s, the beating period is about 6.8927×10⁻¹⁵ s.
Initially P_left≈0.92441. At one quarter of a beating period, cosθ=0 and P_left=0.50. At half a period it is about 0.07559. Total norm and energy probabilities remain unchanged.

check.prompt: At one quarter of the beating period, what is the probability of measuring energy 4E₁?

Quarter of a time period does not mean quarter of an energy probability.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: What changes if an ideal energy measurement has already returned E₂?
apply.answer: The conditioned state is u₂ up to phase. Subsequent free-in-the-well evolution keeps its position density u₂² stationary, and its left-half probability is 1/2. Do not keep using the unmeasured two-mode superposition after that preparation change.

lessons.limits: Ideal hard-wall one-dimensional well, fixed Hamiltonian, coherent two-mode preparation and no intervening measurement unless stated. No environmental decoherence or higher-mode population.

lessons.title: A larger amplitude can carry a smaller transmitted fraction
lessons.idea: Flux, not amplitude height alone, tracks stationary scattering outcomes.
body: Consider a constant-mass particle arriving from the left at a step: V=0 for x<0 and V=V₀ for x>0, with E>V₀>0. Write the left state as e^(ik₁x)+r e^(−ik₁x) and the right state as t_a e^(ik₂x). The incident amplitude is one; t_a is a transmission amplitude, not time.
Continuity of ψ and ψ′ gives 1+r=t_a and k₁(1−r)=k₂t_a. Therefore r=(k₁−k₂)/(k₁+k₂) and t_a=2k₁/(k₁+k₂). Here k₁=√(2mE)/ℏ and k₂=√(2m(E−V₀))/ℏ.

The reflected fraction is R=|r|², while T=(k₂/k₁)|t_a|². The wave-number ratio accounts for the lower velocity on the right. Algebra gives R+T=1; the energy E is unchanged because the step is time independent. Transmitted kinetic energy is E−V₀.

If E<V₀ for a step extending forever to the right, the decaying right-hand solution carries no outgoing stationary current there: T=0. That is not the same setup as a finite barrier with a second face, beyond which a transmitted travelling wave can exist. The width and far boundary matter.
lessons.terms: E, V₀, m, ℏ: Total energy, positive step height, constant particle mass and reduced Planck constant (J or eV consistently; kg; J·s). Convert energies to J when calculating k using SI mass and ℏ. Ratios can use eV consistently. x, k₁, k₂: Position and positive left/right wave numbers (m, m⁻¹, m⁻¹). The above-step setup has E>V₀, so both k values are real. r, t_a, R, T: Reflection/transmission amplitudes and current fractions (no unit). r is not a radial coordinate here. t_a is not time. Reflected current points left; R uses its magnitude. ψ′, i: Spatial derivative and imaginary unit (ψ′ has amplitude per m; i has no unit). A prime differentiates with respect to x; i²=−1. This finite step has no singular point potential. Unit key: m metre (length), s second (time), kg kilogram (mass), N newton (force), J joule (energy), W watt (energy per second), Hz hertz (cycles per second), C coulomb (charge), V volt (joules per coulomb), rad radian (angle). nm=10⁻⁹ m; pm=10⁻¹² m. example.title: Work through one small case
steps: Use E=4.0 eV and V₀=3.0 eV. Then k₂/k₁=√((4−3)/4)=1/2, without needing the particle mass for this ratio.
The amplitudes are r=1/3 and t_a=4/3. Therefore R=1/9≈0.11111 and T=(1/2)(16/9)=8/9≈0.88889.
Although |t_a|>1, the transmitted fraction is below one. The transmitted kinetic energy is 1.0 eV, while the total energy is still 4.0 eV. As V₀→0 at fixed E, k₂/k₁→1, R→0 and T→1.

check.prompt: For the same infinite step, let E approach V₀ from above while V₀ stays positive. What happens to R and T?
explanations: That describes a vanishing step height at fixed energy, not vanishing kinetic energy on the right.
Correct. k₂/k₁ approaches zero, so r approaches one and the transmitted current tends to zero.
Current conservation requires R+T=1; both cannot approach one.

apply.title: Use the idea
apply.text: Does an evanescent tail by itself prove a particle follows a path through a barrier at a particular speed?
apply.answer: No. It is part of a wavefunction solution with stated boundaries. Flux coefficients predict scattering fractions, not individual trajectories or a unique traversal time. A finite-barrier problem also requires matching the second face, unlike the infinite step.

lessons.limits: One-dimensional real stationary step, constant mass, E>V₀ for the displayed travelling-wave coefficients, no absorption and no point singularity. The separately discussed below-step limit is not a finite-barrier formula.

practice.prompt: For the same step geometry, use E=9.0 eV and V₀=8.0 eV. The ratio k₂/k₁=1/3. No absorption is present.
practice.reasoning: Check R+T=1 and explain why |t_a|² alone is not the transmitted fraction. Enter decimal or scientific-notation numbers, not fractions or expressions. Entry tolerances allow rounding; they are not measurement uncertainty.

lessons.title: Use a fresh problem to find the next thing to practise
lessons.idea: Finishing a path records effort; solving a changed problem shows what you can use.
body: First identify the prepared state and the measured quantity. For an observable Â in a normalized state, ⟨A⟩ is its weighted mean and σ_A²=⟨A²⟩−⟨A⟩² is its variance. A variance of zero means the observable is sharp in that state; it does not make every other observable sharp.

For the unchirped Gaussian on the full line, σ_xσ_p=ℏ/2. This is a particular equality case, not a rule for every state. If the width increases during free evolution, keep the actual state’s phase and covariance in mind rather than resetting the equality with the new width.

For an ideal Coulomb orbital, check n≥1,0≤ℓ≤n−1 and |m|≤ℓ before using E_n or angular eigenvalues. For a position interval, include the correct integration measure. A radial density and a volume density have different units and answer different questions.

Try the changed cases below without the worked answer first. Then explain one result in words and name one assumption whose failure would change it. If you need the answer, use that as a specific practice target, not a reason to mark all quantum theory understood. Spin and composite systems, approximation methods and the named advanced extensions remain separate paths.

options: Yes, all components are the same observable
No; different components generally do not commute
explanations: Different components are different operators.

Correct. Their commutators limit joint sharpness; a sharp z component alone does not make x and y sharp.
